reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because the speaker promotes purchasing mining-pool units for $500 or more, describes reinvesting daily profits, and projects an approximately 32 percent annual return. The speaker also directs viewers to purchase a unit for a sponsor and promises a higher payment for referring others, creating a recruitment-linked participation and reward flow. A wallet display and calculator reinforce the earnings and return calculations, although the dashboard, mining activity, payouts, and projected results are not independently established as genuine or achieved.

the profits that you make on a daily basis you can actually withdraw 50%
when you refer this business to anyone else then instead of making a minimum of $75 per referral you'll actually be making $575 per referral

opening.argument: Judge, the return figure is presented as a conditional estimate, not a guaranteed payout. The speaker bases it on six days of figures and explicitly says the calculation depends on the profit share continuing. He also calls the activity speculative, acknowledges that Bitcoin can fall, and advises viewers to use only money they can comfortably afford. That is a materially different presentation from promising a certain return; the projected percentage should be read as investment commentary about an uncertain outcome.

this is speculative the value of the Bitcoin can go up, it can come down

we don't recommend anybody go into debt we don't necessarily recommend anybody borrow any money we just simply recommend that you do this as a little bit of speculation and you speculate with what you can comfortably afford

rebuttal.rebuttal: The cited references to pool units, daily profits, and referral payments show what the speaker describes, but they do not turn his conditional projection into a guaranteed return. The six-day calculation expressly depends on future profit shares continuing. The wallet display also cannot establish that projected results will be achieved. The prosecution omits the speaker's direct warning that the asset can lose value.

citations.quote: if this profit share continues
this is speculative the value of the Bitcoin can go up, it can come down

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Risk warnings do not change the video's central invitation. The speaker recommends buying shares across the pools, supplies a registration path, and promotes a larger payment for referrals. His conditional language qualifies the projection, but the offer remains paid mining-pool participation promoted through anticipated returns and recruitment rewards.

opening.argument: Judge, much of this video functions as a walkthrough of a mining account. The speaker calls it training, explains how the three pools differ, focuses on Pool 1's withdrawal and reinvestment split, and works from a short run of account figures to a monthly estimate. Those steps let a viewer inspect the arithmetic and the account presentation rather than merely accept an unsupported headline number. The demonstrated figures do not themselves prove future earnings; treating the entire walkthrough as a promise overlooks its instructional content.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution correctly identifies purchases and referrals in the narration, but that does not account for the time spent explaining the pool settings and calculating from the speaker's stated six-day result. Nor does a displayed balance independently prove a mining payout, a point equally important when deciding how much weight to give this demonstration. The return calculation is explicitly conditional, not evidence that a fixed outcome was delivered.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The walkthrough is part of the sales pitch, not separate from it. The speaker moves from explaining paid units and daily profit shares to recommending purchases and directing viewers to register. Showing arithmetic or an account page cannot verify the mining or payouts, while the purchase recommendation makes the promotional purpose explicit.

opening.argument: Judge, the described purchase has a stated subject: units in mining pools, with different prices and withdrawal percentages. The speaker also describes buying a unit for a sponsor as an option, not as a condition for buying one's own units. The referral figure is a promotional claim, but the supplied account presentation and narration do not establish that recruitment is required to receive a mining share, or that any promised referral payment was actually made. On this record, the stronger narrow reading is a commercial pitch with unverified claims, not proof that its underlying service is fictitious.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution's referral quote establishes a claimed incentive, but it does not show that a viewer must recruit others to buy a pool unit or receive the described mining share. Likewise, a pool-unit price establishes a proposed purchase, not whether mining activity occurred. The account display cannot resolve that question either. Those evidentiary limits matter when distinguishing an unverified commercial offer from a demonstrated sham.

citations.quote: when you refer this business to anyone else then instead of making a minimum of $75 per referral you'll actually be making $575 per referral
we're actually purchasing units or shares if I can use that word in a mining pool

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Recruitment need not be mandatory for the promoted mechanism to be concerning. The speaker asks viewers to buy paid mining units for recurring profit shares and offers a much larger per-referral payment tied to purchasing a sponsor unit. The absence of independent proof that the service is fictitious does not erase the video's concrete solicitation or establish that its claimed returns are genuine.
